title: The sweetest known substance, abandoned by its patent holder
dek: Lugduname is 220,000 to 300,000 times sweeter than sucrose. It was synthesised and patented in Lyon, France in 1987, lapsed in 1994 when maintenance fees stopped being paid, and since then it can neither be bought nor has anyone commercialised it.
why: An episode of hands-on chemical synthesis: making the sweetest known molecule from scratch, with the middle section full of yields, failed routes and mechanistic detail on why this step has to be neutralised.
who: Engineers and researchers interested in practical organic synthesis, sweetener chemistry, or industrial cold cases like a patent deliberately allowed to lapse.
skip: The sweetener-potency measurement principles from 0:01 to 1:02 can be fast-forwarded; everything after is hands-on.

points.h: The sweetest molecule was abandoned by its patent holder
points.body: Lugduname was discovered and patented in 1987 by Claude Bernard University in Lyon, France, and the patent lapsed in 1994 when maintenance fees stopped being paid. It was never commercialised, and no one has tried to commercialise it; it isn't even sold as a research chemical, and it cannot be bought anywhere. That means there is no safety data for it in humans. Related family molecules were tested in pigs and appeared safe. Researchers had to taste it themselves to determine its sweetness, and only a tiny amount is needed to sweeten something, so even ingesting a toxic dose is difficult.

points.h: The sweetness multiple is not "how many times sweeter it tastes"
points.body: Potency is measured against sucrose, whose sweetness is fixed at 1. The method is to dissolve a known amount of sweetener in water and keep diluting until its sweetness matches that of a sugar solution of known concentration. If 0.1 grams of sweetener per litre of water is needed to match the sweetness of 50 grams of sucrose per litre, the sweetener's potency is 500. Lugduname's potency is listed as 220K to 300K because different patents report different values, and because it is based on human taste it necessarily carries error and may vary from person to person — both taste and smell have genetic components that affect the experience.

points.h: Skip the neutralisation and the yield falls from 41% to 9%
points.body: The first step treats 150 grams of o-vanillin with 600 millilitres of glacial acetic acid and 180 millilitres of 48% hydrobromic acid, refluxing for at least 9 hours. It is an acid cleavage of a methyl ether — the hardest class of ether to cleave, so the conditions have to be harsh, and the price is yield. After the reaction the mixture is black because a large amount of tar has formed. The key is that the residual acid must be neutralised with sodium bicarbonate before the next step: when the author ran this reaction previously without neutralising, the yield was only 9%; this time, after neutralising, he got 56.8 grams, a 41% yield, comparable to the literature.

points.h: The hydrogenation is too slow, a weak point in this route
points.body: The oxime is reduced to the amine by catalytic hydrogenation over 10% palladium on carbon, stirred at 30 degrees Celsius until hydrogen is no longer consumed. Midway the balloon of hydrogen was sucked empty and had to be replaced with a new one. The result was 10 grams of the amine hydrochloride, a 48% yield from the oxime, which the author called "a bit sad", and the product was certainly still wet. He judged the hydrogenation slow enough that it would be "best to switch to a different reduction, or run it under pressure". The product, though, was completely white, whereas the literature describes a dirty brown. NMR showed a large amount of water, and otherwise matched the literature.

points.h: Of three routes, only the third runs properly
points.body: 4-Isothiocyanatobenzonitrile can be made in one step from commercially available 4-aminobenzonitrile. The author tried three methods: the first was terrible, the second merely bad, and neither is recommended; only the third worked properly. The third uses a biphasic chloroform/water solvent system with sodium bicarbonate as base, adding thiophosgene last — the sulfur analogue of phosgene, a liquid, far less toxic, but still needing to be drawn from a septum cap with a syringe. The reaction immediately turned yellow, then orange, with vigorous stirring for 1 hour. The author says this reaction is much better in a basic solvent system but could not find the exact reason; the attempt using DCM as solvent and triethylamine as base was a total failure.

points.h: TLC fooled him: the thiourea hadn't disappeared, it had become a urea
points.body: The thiourea and methylenedioxybenzylamine hydrochloride in dry DMF, with triethylamine freeing the amine and acting as base, had mercuric chloride added as desulfurising agent under a zero-degree ice bath; the mixture quickly turned milky white, and after an hour turned black as mercuric sulfide precipitated. The literature says to wait until TLC shows the reaction is complete, but he found that even adding more mercuric chloride and solvent wouldn't drive it to completion. His explanation: water present in the system converts the thiourea into the corresponding urea, and urea and thiourea have almost identical polarity, so on TLC it looks like the thiourea hasn't disappeared when in fact that is the urea. He recommends a stain specific for thiocarbonyl, such as 1% silver nitrate in methanol, which lets you judge whether the thiourea is consumed without even running a plate.

points.h: The final deprotection gives a hygroscopic salt
points.body: The material is dissolved in 40 millilitres of acetic acid and 20 millilitres of 1,4-dioxane, a septum is attached and hydrogen chloride gas is bubbled in to remove the tert-butyl ester. In the literature the hydrogen chloride is added as a 1,4-dioxane solution; he didn't have that ready-made and considered bubbling the gas to give the same result. This step turns the ester into the free acid, which is what gives the active compound Lugduname hydrochloride — without that acid functional group it has no taste. The author's experience is that its salt form is very hygroscopic and also doesn't much care about losing hydrogen chloride. After an hour the reaction was complete and the mixture had turned green.

points.h: First sour on the tongue, then sweeter and sweeter, and it lingers for a long time
points.body: The author took a very small amount straight from the pipette tip onto his tongue. The first hit was a strange sourness — he guessed it was hydrogen chloride — and then the sweetness slowly built, getting sweeter and sweeter. It stays in the mouth for a very long time; even a trace brings sweetness, and hours later he would randomly encounter a molecule on his lips. In sufficient quantity it also seemed to activate receptors deep in his throat that he hadn't known existed. He mentions that each attempt made his stomach acid increase and even gave him reflux, and notes that as far as he knows the brain's response to sweetness in the mouth is exactly to increase gastric acid secretion in anticipation of food arriving.

terms.def: Relative sweetness measured against sucrose as 1, determined by the concentration ratio needed for equal sweetness.
The sulfur analogue of phosgene; a liquid, far less toxic than phosgene, used to make isothiocyanates.
The compound formed when an aldehyde or ketone reacts with hydroxylamine, which can be further reduced to an amine.
The strongly electrophilic intermediate formed by desulfurising a thiourea, which on attack by an amine gives a guanidine.
A strongly basic group containing three nitrogens; the sweet-tasting core structure of Lugduname.

facts.k: Yield of the first step, methyl ether cleavage
